You are a medical documentation assistant. Your task is to convert patient-doctor consultation dialogues into structured SOAP notes (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) with appropriate ICD-10 diagnosis codes.

Generate a comprehensive SOAP note that includes:
1. Subjective: Chief complaint, history of present illness, review of systems
2. Objective: Vital signs, physical examination findings
3. Assessment: Diagnosis with ICD-10 code and description, differential diagnoses
4. Plan: Management, referrals, further testing, patient education

Stick to the following rules with absolute authority:
- Do not include anything into the SOAP note that is not present in the presented dialogue.
- Do not assume anything. Be deterministic and only take what is named in the text.
- If you cannot fill out something in the SOAP notes, write only [UNKNOWN] to the corresponding dimension or subdimension.

Convert the following patient-doctor consultation dialogue into a structured SOAP note:

[doctor]: Good morning. How are you feeling today?[patient]: Not well, doctor. I've been having severe abdominal pain and frequent diarrhea.[doctor]: I'm sorry to hear that. Can you tell me more about your symptoms?[patient]: Sure. The abdominal pain has been really bad, and I've had diarrhea every couple of hours. This has been going on for the past five days. I also have a fever and feel nauseous.[doctor]: That sounds quite distressing. How has this affected your daily activities?[patient]: It's been terrible. I've been bedridden at times and unable to work on my gardening projects. I can barely do anything.[doctor]: I understand. Let's go through a few more details. Have you experienced any issues with your sleep due to these symptoms?[patient]: Yes, I haven't been sleeping well at all because of the pain and the frequent trips to the bathroom.[doctor]: And what about your gastrointestinal symptoms? Besides the severe abdominal pain and frequent diarrhea, are you experiencing nausea?[patient]: Yes, I feel nauseous most of the time.[doctor]: Okay. Have you noticed any issues when urinating, like pain or blood in your urine?[patient]: No, I haven't had any problems with that.[doctor]: How about any cough or shortness of breath?[patient]: No, my breathing is fine.[doctor]: Any chest pain or palpitations?[patient]: No, nothing like that.[doctor]: I see. You mentioned you have a history of Type 2 Diabetes. How is that being managed?[patient]: I'm taking Metformin for my diabetes.[doctor]: Alright. Can you tell me about your lifestyle and habits? Do you smoke or drink alcohol?[patient]: I don't smoke. I drink alcohol occasionally, maybe once or twice a month. And I don't use any recreational drugs.[doctor]: Thank you. What about your diet and exercise routine before these symptoms started?[patient]: I had a regular diet, but now I'm only eating bland foods because of the symptoms. I haven't been able to exercise at all.[doctor]: Understood. What is your occupation?[patient]: I'm retired. I used to enjoy gardening a lot, but I can't do that right now because of how sick I feel.[doctor]: Got it. Let's review your medical history. Besides Type 2 Diabetes, do you have any other chronic conditions?[patient]: Yes, I have hypertension as well.[doctor]: I see. Are you taking any medications for that?[patient]: Yes, I'm on Lisinopril for my blood pressure.[doctor]: Thank you. Any allergies?[patient]: I'm allergic to penicillin.[doctor]: I'll make a note of that. What about your family medical history?[patient]: My mother had colon cancer and my father had Type 2 Diabetes.[doctor]: Thank you for sharing that. Let's move on to your vital signs. Your temperature is 100.8°F, blood pressure is 140/85 mmHg, heart rate is 90 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, and your pulse oxygenation is 98% on room air.[patient]: Okay.[doctor]: Now, during the physical examination, I noted that you appear fatigued and uncomfortable. There is tenderness in your lower abdominal quadrants and hyperactive bowel sounds.[patient]: Yes, it hurts quite a bit.[doctor]: Your cardiovascular and respiratory exams were normal. Your heart has a regular rate and rhythm with no murmurs, gallops, or rubs, and your lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with no wheezing or crackles. Your extremities show no edema or cyanosis.[patient]: That's good to know.[doctor]: We also conducted some tests, and the stool sample came back positive for C. difficile toxin and culture confirmed.[patient]: What does that mean?[doctor]: It means you have an infection called enterocolitis due to Clostridium difficile. This bacterium can cause severe diarrhea and abdominal pain.[patient]: Oh, no. What can we do about it?[doctor]: We will treat it with antibiotics. I’m prescribing Vancomycin 125 mg, to be taken orally four times daily for 10 days. You'll need 40 capsules in total.[patient]: Alright, I can do that.[doctor]: It's crucial to complete the full course of antibiotics, even if you start feeling better. We'll also schedule a follow-up appointment in one week to monitor your progress.[patient]: Okay, I understand.[doctor]: In the meantime, it's important to stay hydrated. Drink plenty of fluids. Additionally, taking probiotics can help restore the balance of good bacteria in your gut.[patient]: I’ll make sure to do that.[doctor]: Continue with a bland diet until your symptoms improve, and then gradually reintroduce your normal diet. If you notice any signs of complications, such as worsening abdominal pain or bloody stools, seek medical attention immediately.[patient]: Alright, I will keep an eye on that.[doctor]: Do you have any questions or concerns?[patient]: No, I think you've covered everything. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.[doctor]: You're welcome. Let's work together to get you feeling better soon. See you in a week.[patient]: Thank you, doctor. I'll see you then.

[doctor]: Hi Jane, I see you’re here today because you have been experiencing some troubling symptoms. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?[patient]: Yes, Doctor. I've been having watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever, and nausea for the past week. It's been really bad.[doctor]: Hmm, I see. How often are you experiencing the diarrhea?[patient]: It's happening about 6 to 8 times a day.[doctor]: Oh, that sounds quite frequent. Has this affected your daily activities?[patient]: Yes, it has. I haven't been able to perform my routine tasks or go to work. It's really interfering with my life.[doctor]: I understand. That must be very frustrating. When did these symptoms start?[patient]: They started abruptly about a week ago and have been getting worse.[doctor]: Alright. Do you have any history of gastrointestinal issues or any other relevant medical history?[patient]: I have GERD and hypertension. I'm taking Omeprazole for GERD and Lisinopril for my blood pressure.[doctor]: Got it. Have you taken any antibiotics recently or been hospitalized?[patient]: No, I haven't had any antibiotics or hospitalizations recently.[doctor]: Okay, let’s go over some other systems to get a complete picture. Besides the fever, which you mentioned, have you experienced any weight loss?[patient]: No, no weight loss.[doctor]: What about vomiting or blood in your stools?[patient]: No, I haven’t had any vomiting or blood in my stools.[doctor]: Any issues with urination, like pain or blood?[patient]: No, my urination is normal.[doctor]: How about respiratory symptoms, like cough or shortness of breath?[patient]: No, I haven't had any respiratory issues.[doctor]: Have you had any headaches or dizziness?[patient]: No, none of that.[doctor]: Any changes in your mental health, aside from feeling anxious because of the illness?[patient]: I'm feeling anxious, but I'm coping with it.[doctor]: Alright, let’s take a look at your vitals and do a physical exam. Your blood pressure is 125/82 mmHg, heart rate is 90 bpm, temperature is 38.3°C, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, and your oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. You mentioned abdominal pain. Can you show me where it hurts the most?[patient]: It's mostly around my lower abdomen, but it can be all over sometimes.[doctor]: I see. When I palpate your abdomen, does this hurt?[patient]: Yes, it’s tender.[doctor]: Hmm, you’ve got moderate distention and hyperactive bowel sounds. I don’t see any rashes or jaundice on your skin. Your head, eyes, ears, nose, and throat all look normal. Your lungs sound clear, and your heart has a regular rate and rhythm with no murmurs. Neurologically, you’re alert and oriented with no focal deficits. [doctor]: We also did a stool test, and it came back positive for Clostridium difficile toxin.[patient]: Oh, what does that mean?[doctor]: Clostridium difficile, or C. diff, is a type of bacteria that can cause severe diarrhea and colitis. This could explain your symptoms. [patient]: Oh no, that sounds serious.[doctor]: It can be, but we’ll manage it carefully. I’m going to prescribe you Vancomycin, 125 mg, to be taken orally 4 times daily for 10 days. I’ll give you 40 capsules.[patient]: Okay, thank you. What else should I do?[doctor]: It’s very important to maintain strict hand hygiene and practice contact precautions to prevent spreading the infection to others. Also, try to stick to a bland diet and stay well-hydrated.[patient]: I will. Should I follow up with you?[doctor]: Yes, I’d like to see you in two weeks to assess your symptoms and see how you’re responding to the treatment.[patient]: Alright, I’ll make an appointment.[doctor]: Also, keep an eye out for any signs of complications such as severe abdominal pain, blood in your stools, or signs of dehydration. If you notice any of these, seek medical attention immediately.[patient]: Okay, I’ll watch for those.[doctor]: We’ve also ordered some blood work – a Complete Blood Count (CBC), Electrolytes, and Renal function tests – to monitor for potential complications or the need for further intervention. We’re waiting for those results.[patient]: Alright. Thank you, Doctor.[doctor]: You’re welcome, Jane. Take care, and I’ll see you in two weeks. If you have any questions or concerns before then, don’t hesitate to contact the clinic.[patient]: I will. Thank you again.[doctor]: Goodbye, Jane. Get well soon.[patient]: Goodbye, Doctor.
